newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW--Waste Management CEO sticking to plan.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW--Waste Management CEO sticking to plan.

text.p: Ronald LeMay said Monday his immediate task as the new leader of Waste Management Inc will be to execute a restructuring plan set in motion five months ago by his predecessor.

After a two-month learning period, the former Sprint Corp executive said, he will feel free to begin making his own mark at Oak Brook, Ill.-based Waste Management, the largest U.S. garbage hauling and handling firm.

"It's probably going to take me 60 days to get my feet on the ground ... It's not that there will be a plan in 60 days, or that we're gearing a bunch of changes around some 60-day deadline. It's just that, as a practical matter, I'm going to need that kind of time," he said in an interview with Reuters.
Shares in Waste Management turned down 1-1/4 to 31-3/4 in heavy volume on a broadly lower market Monday after the naming of LeMay as chairman, president and chief executive.
Major shareholders and analysts greeted the appointment as a welcome end to an arduous five-month CEO search.
Soros Fund Management, which owns a large stake in the company, issued a statement supporting the LeMay appointment.

"The single biggest thing WMX needed was new, aggressive, no-holds-barred leadership to help it figure out how to generate more cash flow from its assets. I believe LeMay can get that done," said Goldman Sachs analyst Barry Mannis.
Argus Research analyst James Kelleher said, "This ship's been rudderless so long, it was time to get somebody in there and I think they got a pretty good guy."

He said WMX wanted "to bring in somebody from outside the company culture so he could fire some top managers. They probably really wanted somebody to come in and shake up the ranks. That's why they made a point of shopping not just outside the company, but outside the industry."

Headhunting firm Heidrick & Struggles screened 30 candidates for the job -- all from outside the trash business. Six were ultimately sent to the company's search committee, said Heidrick & Struggles vice-chairman John Thompson.
LeMay replaces Phillip Rooney, who resigned as CEO in February under pressure from Soros and other major investors, but not before he designed a broad restructuring plan.
The plan calls for Waste Management to divest $1.5 billion in assets, cut capital spending, eliminate 3,000 jobs and make other sweeping changes, some of which have been accomplished.

LeMay said he has a broad mandate from the board, but he expects no immediate management shake-up. "It would delight me if we could get this done with the senior management team that exists here, but I have no constraint imposed on me," he said.

Formerly president and chief operating officer of Sprint, LeMay said he comes to Waste Management with no experience in the trash business, but he said he sees parallels between it and telecommunications. "They are both large businesses which require a huge concentration on cost management," he said.

At Sprint, LeMay's rise to the top was blocked by chairman and CEO William Esrey, his well-entrenched 57-year-old boss, likely influencing his decision to take the Waste Management job, analysts said. In response, LeMay said, "I chose to do this because I saw an opportunity to be the chairman and CEO of a large, world-class company ... Bill Esry, as chairman and CEO of Sprint, has no plans to leave anytime soon. He is a great friend of mine, doing a fantastic job."
Details of LeMay's reportedly lucrative compensation plan are being ironed out but will be disclosed soon, WMX said.
"My interests will clearly be aligned with the interests of shareholders," LeMay said of his pay package.
